opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's an incredibly important effort, and also an incredibly difficult one. Let me explain why I hold both of those views at once.

In the era before generative AI, when we were talking about responsible AI and things like fairness, we were mostly dealing with models that had a fairly narrow, well-defined task. You'd have a consumer lending model, and the output was essentially a yes or no, or a probability of default. In that setting, it's relatively straightforward to say what you mean by fairness. You can say, "I want the false rejection rate to be approximately equal across racial groups," and then you can go measure it. There are definitional debates, of course, and there are known tensions between different fairness notions, but at least you can write the thing down mathematically and audit for it.

Generative AI really blows that up, because the space of inputs and outputs is essentially open-ended. If I ask a large language model to write a story or summarize a document or answer a medical question, what does it even mean for that output to be "fair"? Or "private"? Or "non-toxic"? The use cases are so broad that a single, universal definition becomes very hard to pin down. So in some sense, we've gone from a world where the science was ahead of the practice to a world where the practice is way ahead of the science.

That's why I think standardization efforts are valuable. If every company and every research group is using its own private benchmarks, its own definitions, its own red-teaming protocols, then you can't really compare claims. One firm says their model is "safer" and another says theirs is "more truthful," and nobody can tell what those statements actually mean. Shared benchmarks, shared evaluation methodologies, and some agreement on terminology at least give us a common language.

But I'd add a couple of cautions. One is the classic concern that once a benchmark becomes the target, people optimize for it, and it stops measuring the thing you cared about. We've seen that across machine learning for decades, and with LLMs there's the added problem that benchmark data can leak into training sets. So I think any standardization effort has to be dynamic. It has to evolve, include held-out evaluation, and involve adversarial testing rather than just static leaderboards.

The second caution is that I think responsible AI for generative models is going to have to become much more use-case specific. Rather than asking "Is this foundation model fair?" in the abstract, I think the more productive question is "Is this model, deployed in this application, with these guardrails, behaving in the way we want for this population of users?" That's a narrower question, but it's one we can actually get scientific traction on.

So overall I'm encouraged. There's a lot of serious work happening, in industry, in academia, and in government bodies like NIST, and I think that convergence is healthy. But I'd encourage people to be humble about it. We're still very early in developing the science of measuring these systems, and I think we should be skeptical of anyone who claims they've solved it.

r001.rationale: The response says the field is “very early in developing the science of measuring these systems,” directly framing standardized metrics as an early-stage effort.

r002.rationale: It notes definitional debates and tensions for narrow tasks, but describes fairness as relatively straightforward to define and audit; it does not say that sufficient metric coverage remains unresolved for those tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a really important effort, and I also think it's a very hard problem, maybe harder than people appreciate. Let me try to unpack that a bit.

If you go back a few years, the predictive machine learning world had a relatively clean story around measurement. You had a model, you had a held-out test set, you had a well-defined loss function, and you could say with a straight face, "this model has such-and-such accuracy on this distribution." And then on the responsible AI side, at least for things like fairness, we had a decent toolkit too. You could ask whether the false positive rate was equalized across demographic groups, you could measure demographic parity, and so on. Those definitions had their problems, and reasonable people could argue about which one was right for a given application, but at least they were quantitative, they were well-posed, and you could audit a system against them.

Generative AI breaks a lot of that. The first problem is that the output space is just enormous and open-ended. If I ask a language model to summarize a document or write a piece of code or give me medical advice, there isn't a single right answer sitting in a test set that I can compare against. So the notion of "performance" itself becomes much fuzzier, and we end up with proxies, whether that's benchmarks like MMLU or human preference ratings or using another LLM as a judge, and every one of those proxies has known weaknesses. Benchmarks get contaminated, because the test questions leak into the training data. Human ratings are noisy and expensive and often measure something closer to "sounds confident" than "is correct." And LLM-as-judge inherits whatever biases the judging model has.

The second problem, and this is the one I spend more time thinking about, is on the responsible AI side. In the predictive setting, you could define fairness because you had a clear notion of a decision and a clear notion of harm: you denied someone a loan, you didn't. With a generative model, what does it even mean for the output to be fair, or safe, or non-toxic? These are notions that are inherently contextual, they depend on who's asking and why, and in many cases there's genuine disagreement among people about what the right behavior is. So standardizing the measurement of something that we can't fully define is tricky. You risk measuring the measurable rather than the important.

Now, having said all that, I don't think the answer is to throw up our hands. I'd make a few observations about what I think good standardization looks like.

One is that it should be modular and application-specific rather than one giant score. The things you care about for a customer service chatbot are quite different from the things you care about for a code assistant or a model used in a clinical setting. So I'm more optimistic about standards that look like, here is a battery of tests for this class of use cases, than about a single leaderboard number that's supposed to tell you whether a model is "responsible."

The second is that measurement needs to be adversarial and ongoing rather than a one-time certification. These models are being deployed in environments where people are actively trying to get them to misbehave. So a static benchmark run once before release doesn't tell you much. Red-teaming, continual monitoring, and the ability to update the evaluation as new failure modes are discovered are all essential, and I'd like to see standards bodies think about that lifecycle view rather than a snapshot.

And third, and this is maybe my broader point, I think there's a real role for the more mathematical, algorithmic community here, the people who come out of learning theory and algorithmic game theory, to try to put these notions on firmer footing. Not because we'll find the one true definition of a safe language model, but because being precise about what you're measuring, what assumptions you're making, and what guarantees you can and can't provide is itself a form of responsibility. A lot of what gets labeled "responsible AI" right now is really a set of good intentions and some ad hoc checks. Standardization is only going to be meaningful if it rests on definitions that are rigorous enough that you can actually test whether a system meets them, and honest enough that you know what they leave out.

So, long answer, but I'd summarize it as: necessary, hard, and we should be very wary of premature consensus on metrics that are convenient to compute but don't capture what we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response calls standardizing generative-AI metrics hard and warns against premature consensus, but does not attribute the expected evolution of metrics to the field being at an early stage.

r002.rationale: It describes traditional predictive-task metrics as relatively clean and quantitative, with some definitional problems, but does not say sufficient metric coverage remains unresolved even for narrow predictive tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think standardization is useful, but we have to be clear about what a measurement actually tells us. Even with predictive accuracy, a benchmark measures performance on a particular distribution of examples. It doesn’t automatically tell you how a model will behave in the application where you’re going to deploy it.

With responsible AI, that gets more complicated because we’re talking about multiple properties—fairness, privacy, robustness—and those properties need definitions. Fairness with respect to whom? Privacy against what kind of adversary? Those aren’t questions you can resolve simply by collecting more benchmark scores.

Generative AI adds another layer because the space of possible outputs is so broad, and whether an output is appropriate can depend heavily on context. The same behavior might be acceptable in a creative writing tool and quite problematic in a medical setting.

So I’m supportive of developing common evaluation methods. They let us compare systems and make claims more precise. But I’d be cautious about turning those evaluations into a single stamp of approval. We need to understand what’s being tested, what’s being left out, and how the results relate to actual use. And we need continued evaluation after deployment, because passing a benchmark is only one piece of the evidence.

r001.rationale: The response supports common evaluation methods and cautions against treating them as approval, but does not attribute metric development to the field’s early stage.

r002.rationale: It notes that benchmarks cover particular example distributions, but does not say sufficient metric coverage remains unresolved even for traditional narrow predictive tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think these efforts are valuable, but we have to be careful about what we expect a standard to accomplish. With language models, even defining performance is difficult. Are we measuring factual accuracy, usefulness, the ability to follow instructions? And responsible AI adds other dimensions—privacy, fairness, the potential for harmful outputs—that aren’t necessarily captured by the same test.

There’s also a distinction between evaluating a model in isolation and evaluating the system in which it’s deployed. The same model can have very different consequences depending on who’s using it, what tools it has access to, and what decisions people make based on its output.

So I’d welcome standards that make evaluations more transparent and comparable. But I’d be skeptical of a single score or a certification that says, essentially, “This model is responsible.” We need multiple measurements, explicit assumptions about the setting, and continued evaluation as the technology and its uses change.

r001.rationale: The response discusses difficulties in defining LLM performance and responsible-AI measures, but does not attribute the challenge to the field being at an early stage.
